props.title: I, Daniel Blake

sections.content: **I, Daniel Blake** (2016) represents Ken Loach's most powerful indictment of bureaucratic cruelty in modern Britain. The film follows a 59-year-old carpenter caught in an impossible situation: too ill to work but too "healthy" according to rigid government assessments to qualify for benefits. Like Loach's earlier **Kes** (1969) and **Ladybird Ladybird** (1994), it captures working-class struggles with documentary-like authenticity. The film's raw power comes from Dave Johns' devastating performance as Daniel and his friendship with Katie (Hayley Squires), a single mother similarly trapped by the system. Their supermarket scene, where Katie breaks down at a food bank, delivers one of cinema's most heartbreaking moments of recent years.

sections.content: This style of social realist cinema traces back to Britain's kitchen sink dramas of the 1960s, with films like **This Sporting Life** (1963) and **Poor Cow** (1967) documenting working-class life with unflinching honesty. Modern filmmakers like Andrea Arnold with **Fish Tank** (2009) and Shane Meadows with **This Is England** (2006) have carried this tradition forward. The approach relies on naturalistic performances, often from non-professional actors, and a documentary-style aesthetic that emphasizes authenticity over artifice. SUBHEAD: The New Wave of Social Commentary Cinema

Recent years have seen a global surge in films tackling systemic inequality. **Parasite** (2019) uses dark comedy to expose class warfare in South Korea, while **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) employs magical realism to critique American capitalism. **The Florida Project** (2017) shares I, Daniel Blake's concern for society's most vulnerable, following struggling families living in budget motels. These films demonstrate how contemporary cinema continues to serve as a powerful tool for social criticism and humanitarian advocacy.
